opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the era they grew up in and what that forced them to become.

Professor Tu, Zhuowen, was my PhD advisor at UCSD, so I'm obviously biased. But I think his generation is genuinely special. They came up in computer vision before deep learning took over, at a time when nothing really worked. You couldn't throw a big network and a huge dataset at a problem and get a strong result. You had to think very hard about what the problem actually *is*. What does it mean to parse an image? What is the structure of a scene? How do you formulate that mathematically, as a probabilistic model, or as inference over some representation? That lineage, including people like Song-Chun Zhu and the broader UCLA school Professor Tu came from, was very ambitious. They wanted a unified, principled theory of vision, not just a better number on a benchmark.

What I admire is that they kept that ambition but weren't dogmatic. When deep learning arrived, a lot of people from that generation either resisted it or abandoned everything they had believed. Professor Tu did neither. He embraced the new tools very quickly, but he brought the old way of thinking with him. Some of the work we did together, like deeply supervised nets or holistically-nested edge detection, came from that mindset: asking what kind of supervision and structure a network should have, rather than just making it bigger. That intuition came from years of thinking about the problem before the tools existed.

There's also something about their character. They did research when it wasn't fashionable and there was no money or hype. You only did computer vision then because you were curious about the problem. That kind of intrinsic motivation is rarer now. Today the field moves so fast and is so crowded that it's easy to just chase the next trend. When I talk with people like Professor Tu, I'm reminded that the real questions, like how a machine can understand the visual world the way we do, are still open. Scaling hasn't fully answered them. Their generation never lost sight of that, and I think it's something we should inherit.

r002.rationale: It describes the pre-deep-learning era and the need for careful problem formulation, but does not say researchers built systems from scratch because supporting software infrastructure was unavailable.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe Professor Tu or his peers opening the previously insular CVPR community to later researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
Professor Tu was my PhD advisor at UCSD, and I think the reason I respect him and that whole generation so much is that they were doing computer vision when it was genuinely hard, and when almost nobody outside the field believed it would work.

You have to remember the context. Before deep learning, before ImageNet really changed everything, vision was this very fragmented, almost craft-like discipline. You hand-designed features, you built graphical models, you worried about inference algorithms, you thought very carefully about the structure of the problem. People like Zhuowen Tu, Song-Chun Zhu, Alan Yuille, Jitendra Malik, Fei-Fei Li, that whole lineage, they were asking the deep questions: what is an image, what is a representation, how does perception relate to reasoning. They were thinking in terms of generative and discriminative models, Bayesian frameworks, what the right priors should be. A lot of that was very principled, very mathematical, and honestly very difficult work, with results that were often modest by today's standards.

And then the field changed almost overnight. Many of the tools they spent a decade building were, in some sense, swept away by big data and big compute. I think a lesser generation would have become bitter about that. What impressed me about Professor Tu was that he didn't. He embraced it. He moved into deep learning early, and some of the work we did together, like deeply supervised nets and holistically nested edge detection, came directly out of that transition. He was bringing old intuitions about multi-scale structure and supervision into the new paradigm, rather than pretending the new paradigm didn't exist.

The other thing I'd say is that he taught me taste. When I was a student, I would get excited about tricks, about getting a number up on a benchmark. He would always push back and ask, what is the real insight here, what did we actually learn. That instinct to look past the leaderboard, to care about whether something is a genuine idea, that comes from the era he grew up in, where you couldn't hide behind scale. You had to have an idea.

So when I look at that generation, I see people who built the foundations, who had the intellectual honesty to accept being disrupted, and who then kept contributing anyway. I think that's a model of how to be a scientist, and it's something I try to carry forward with my own students at NYU.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Xie's focus on tricks and benchmark scores as a student with Professor Tu pushing him to ask what the real insight was, describing how Tu taught him research judgment.

r002.rationale: It describes early computer vision as fragmented and craft-like, but does not say the generation had to build research systems from scratch because supporting software infrastructure was unavailable.

r003.rationale: It credits Tu's generation with building foundations, but does not say they opened the previously insular CVPR community to later researchers.

astra-6.text:
What I really admire is their willingness to tackle the fundamental questions. What does it mean for a machine to see? How do you represent an image, and how do you connect that representation to an understanding of the world? Those are difficult questions, especially when you don’t have today’s data or computing resources.

Professor Tu and that generation of researchers approached vision with a very broad intellectual toolkit. They were thinking about learning, statistics, structure, and perception together. To me, that reflects a depth of curiosity that goes beyond making a particular benchmark number better.

That’s the spirit I respect: choosing a problem because it matters, and trying to develop an idea that explains something. The tools change, sometimes dramatically, but that kind of scientific taste remains valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
What I admire is the way that generation approached research. Computer vision was much less mature, and they had to think deeply about what the problems were, not just how to improve a number on a benchmark. They drew connections between mathematics, statistics, and how we perceive the world.

For me, Professor Tu represents that kind of intellectual curiosity and rigor. You can learn a particular technique from someone, but learning how to choose a problem, question your assumptions, and develop your own taste—that has a much longer-lasting influence. That’s why I hold them in such high regard.
